sectionTitle: Forces and motion: Describing motion along a line

specStatements.text: Distance is how far an object moves. Distance does not involve direction. Distance is a scalar quantity.

Displacement includes both the distance an object moves, measured in a straight line from the start point to the finish point and the direction of that straight line. Displacement is a vector quantity.
Students should be able to express a displacement in terms of both the magnitude and direction.
Speed does not involve direction. Speed is a scalar quantity.
The speed of a moving object is rarely constant. When people walk, run or travel in a car their speed is constantly changing.
The speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle depends on many factors including: age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled.
Typical values may be taken as:
walking ̴ 1.5 m/s
running ̴ 3 m/s
cycling ̴ 6 m/s.
Students should be able to recall typical values of speed for a person walking, running and cycling as well as the typical values of speed for different types of transportation systems.
It is not only moving objects that have varying speed. The speed of sound and the speed of the wind also vary.
A typical value for the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s.
Students should be able to make measurements of distance and time and then calculate speed s of objects.
For an object moving at constant speed the distance travelled in a specific time can be calculated using the equation:
distance travelled = speed × time
[s = v t]
distance, s, in metres, m
speed, v, in metres per second, m/s
time, t, in seconds, s
Students should be able to calculate average speed for non-uniform motion.
The velocity of an object is its speed in a given direction. Velocity is a vector quantity.
Students should be able to explain the vector–scalar distinction as it applies to displacement, distance, velocity and speed.
(HT only) Students should be able to explain qualitatively, with examples, that motion in a circle involves constant speed but changing velocity.
If an object moves along a straight line, the distance travelled can be represented by a distance–time graph.
The speed of an object can be calculated from the gradient of its distance–time graph.
(HT only) If an object is accelerating, its speed at any particular time can be determined by drawing a tangent and measuring the gradient of the distance–time graph at that time.

Students should be able to draw distance–time graphs from measurements and extract and interpret lines and slopes of distance–time graphs, translating information between graphical and numerical form.
Students should be able to determine speed from a distance–time graph.
The average acceleration of an object can be calculated using the equation:
acceleration = (change in velocity)/(time taken)
acceleration, a, in metres per second squared, m/s^2
change in velocity, ∆ v, in metres per second, m/s
time, t, in seconds, s
An object that slows down is decelerating.
Students should be able to estimate the magnitude of everyday accelerations.
The acceleration of an object can be calculated from the gradient of a velocity–time graph.
(HT only) The distance travelled by an object (or displacement of an object) can be calculated from the area under a velocity–time graph.
Students should be able to:
• draw velocity–time graphs from measurements and interpret lines and slopes to determine acceleration
• (HT only) interpret enclosed areas in velocity–time graphs to determine distance travelled (or displacement)
• (HT only) measure, when appropriate, the area under a velocity–time graph by counting squares.
The following equation applies to uniform acceleration:
(final velocity)^2 - (initial velocity)^2 = 2 × acceleration × distance
final velocity, v, in metres per second, m/s
initial velocity, u, in metres per second, m/s
acceleration, a, in metres per second squared, m/s^2
distance, s, in metres, m
Near the Earth’s surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2.
An object falling through a fluid initially accelerates due to the force of gravity. Eventually the resultant force will be zero and the object will move at its terminal velocity.
(Physics only) Students should be able to:
• draw and interpret velocity–time graphs for objects that reach terminal velocity
• interpret the changing motion in terms of the forces acting.

concepts.definition: Distance is how far an object moves along the path it actually travels. It does not involve direction, so it is a scalar quantity: a magnitude and a unit fully describe it, for example 450 m.

Displacement is the distance an object moves measured in a straight line from the start point to the finish point, together with the direction of that straight line. It is quoted as a magnitude and a direction, for example 450 m due east.
A scalar quantity has magnitude only. Distance and speed are scalars: stating the number and the unit says everything there is to say about them.
A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction. Displacement and velocity are vectors: two vectors of the same size pointing different ways are different quantities.
Speed is how fast an object is moving. It does not involve direction, so speed is a scalar quantity, measured in metres per second, m/s.
The specification gives typical values that may be taken as: walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s. These are estimates to be recalled and used, not exact figures.

Students should also be able to recall typical speeds for different types of transportation system, for example a car on a motorway at roughly 30 m/s, a train at roughly 50 m/s and an aeroplane at roughly 250 m/s.
The speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle depends on many factors including age, terrain, fitness and the distance travelled.

The speed of a moving object is rarely constant: when people walk, run or travel in a car their speed changes constantly. It is not only moving objects that have varying speed, because the speed of sound and the speed of the wind also vary.
A typical value for the speed of sound in air is 330 m/s. The actual value varies, for example with the temperature of the air.
Speed is found by measuring a distance, for example with a ruler, tape measure or trundle wheel, measuring the time taken with a stopwatch or light gates, and then dividing the distance by the time.
For an object moving at constant speed the distance travelled in a specific time can be calculated using distance travelled = speed × time, written in symbols as [s = v t].

concepts.term: Quantities and units in [s = v t]
concepts.definition: In s = v t the distance s is in metres, m; the speed v is in metres per second, m/s; and the time t is in seconds, s.
For non-uniform motion the average speed is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken, including any time spent stationary.
The velocity of an object is its speed in a given direction, so velocity is a vector quantity. Two objects with equal speeds have different velocities if they move in different directions.
Distance and speed are scalars; displacement and velocity are the matching vector quantities. Each pair has the same unit, and the vector member of the pair also carries a direction.

An object moving in a circle at a steady rate has constant speed but changing velocity, because its direction of motion changes continuously. Examples include a car on a roundabout and a satellite in a circular orbit.
If an object moves along a straight line, the distance travelled can be represented by a distance-time graph, with time on the horizontal axis and distance on the vertical axis.

The speed of an object can be calculated from the gradient of its distance-time graph: gradient is the change in distance divided by the change in time. A horizontal line has zero gradient, so the object is stationary.

concepts.term: Tangent to a distance-time graph (HT only)
concepts.definition: If an object is accelerating, its speed at any particular time can be determined by drawing a tangent to the curve at that time and measuring the gradient of that tangent.
Students should be able to draw distance-time graphs from measurements, and extract and interpret lines and slopes, translating information between graphical and numerical form.
The average acceleration of an object can be calculated using acceleration = (change in velocity)/(time taken), written in symbols as [a = (∆v)/(t)].
Acceleration, a, is in metres per second squared, m/s^2; change in velocity, ∆ v, is in metres per second, m/s; and time, t, is in seconds, s.
An object that slows down is decelerating. Its acceleration has the opposite sign to its velocity, so for an object moving forwards the acceleration is negative.
Students should be able to estimate the magnitude of everyday accelerations, for example a family car pulling away at roughly 2 m/s^2 and an object falling freely at about 9.8 m/s^2.

The acceleration of an object can be calculated from the gradient of a velocity-time graph. Students should be able to draw velocity-time graphs from measurements and interpret lines and slopes to determine acceleration.

concepts.term: Area under a velocity-time graph (HT only)
concepts.definition: The distance travelled by an object, or the displacement of an object, can be calculated from the area under a velocity-time graph, and students should be able to interpret enclosed areas to determine it.
Where the area under a velocity-time graph is not a simple triangle or rectangle, it can be measured, when appropriate, by counting squares and multiplying by the quantity one square represents.
The following equation applies to uniform acceleration: (final velocity)^2 - (initial velocity)^2 = 2 × acceleration × distance, written in symbols as [v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s].

concepts.term: Quantities and units in [v^2 - u^2 = 2 a s]
concepts.definition: Final velocity v and initial velocity u are in metres per second, m/s; acceleration a is in metres per second squared, m/s^2; and distance s is in metres, m.
Near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2, whatever its mass.

An object falling through a fluid initially accelerates due to the force of gravity. As it speeds up the drag force grows until eventually the resultant force is zero and the object moves at its terminal velocity. Physics only: students should be able to draw and interpret velocity-time graphs for objects that reach terminal velocity and interpret the changing motion in terms of the forces acting.

misconceptions.question: A student walks 30 m east along a corridor and then walks 30 m back to the start. What is her displacement?
misconceptions.correct: Zero, because the finish point is the start point, so the straight line joining them has no length.
misconceptions.misconception: Distance and displacement are two names for the same thing, so the displacement must also be 60 m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities are lengths in metres, and in the first examples students meet - a single straight walk from A to B - the two numbers really are equal, so the difference never has to be noticed.
misconceptions.correction: Distance is measured along the whole path travelled; displacement is measured in a straight line from start to finish and includes direction. Out and back gives 60 m of distance but zero displacement.

misconceptions.question: A ship sails 12 km from a harbour and ends up due south of it. How should its displacement be written?
misconceptions.correct: 12 km due south of the harbour - the magnitude and the direction are both needed.
misconceptions.misconception: Writing '12 km' on its own is a complete answer for a displacement.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Almost every number a student writes in science is a magnitude and a unit, so the habit of stopping there is very strong, and a direction feels like extra description rather than part of the value.
misconceptions.correction: A displacement is a vector, so it is only fully expressed when both the magnitude and the direction of the straight line from start to finish are given.

misconceptions.question: A walker goes 3.0 km due east and then 4.0 km due north. What is the magnitude of the displacement?
misconceptions.correct: 5.0 km, found from the right-angled triangle: the square root of (3.0^2 + 4.0^2).
misconceptions.misconception: 7.0 km, because the two legs are simply added together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Adding is what students do with distances, and the two legs are given in the same unit, so arithmetic addition feels like the obvious move.
misconceptions.correction: Displacements at right angles combine like the sides of a right-angled triangle, not by simple addition. Here the magnitude is 5.0 km and the direction must be stated as well.

misconceptions.question: Is speed a scalar or a vector quantity?
misconceptions.correct: Speed is a scalar quantity, because it does not involve direction.
misconceptions.misconception: Speed must be a vector because a moving object is obviously going somewhere.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students confuse the direction the object happens to be travelling with whether direction is part of the quantity itself. A car has a direction, but its speedometer reading does not.
misconceptions.correction: Speed tells you only how fast, never which way; that makes it a scalar. Velocity is the vector that carries the direction as well.

misconceptions.question: A car is driven across a town. Is its speed constant?
misconceptions.correct: No. The speed of a moving object is rarely constant; it changes at junctions, bends and traffic.
misconceptions.misconception: Once a vehicle is moving it travels at one steady speed for the whole journey.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Textbook problems nearly always specify a constant speed so that s = v t can be used, so students come to treat constant speed as the normal case rather than a simplification.
misconceptions.correction: Real journeys involve constant changes of speed, which is why average speed - total distance divided by total time - is needed.

misconceptions.question: What is a typical speed for a person walking?
misconceptions.correct: About 1.5 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: About 15 m/s, because walking feels quite fast.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students have little feel for the size of metres per second and do not check the value against experience, so an answer ten times too large passes unnoticed.
misconceptions.correction: Typical values are walking about 1.5 m/s, running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s; 15 m/s is closer to a car in a town.

misconceptions.question: Which is faster, a typical runner or a typical cyclist?
misconceptions.correct: The cyclist, at about 6 m/s, compared with about 3 m/s for the runner.
misconceptions.misconception: The two are about the same, or the runner is faster.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The typical values are learned as a list of three numbers with no physical anchor, so which number belongs to which activity is easily swapped.
misconceptions.correction: The typical values increase in the order walking 1.5 m/s, running 3 m/s, cycling 6 m/s - each roughly double the one before.

misconceptions.question: What is a typical value for the speed of sound in air?
misconceptions.correct: About 330 m/s, though the actual value varies.
misconceptions.misconception: Sound travels at a single fixed speed, or at the speed of light.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Sound seems to arrive instantly over short distances, and 'the speed of sound' is spoken of as though it were one unchanging constant.
misconceptions.correction: A typical value is 330 m/s, but the speed of sound in air varies, for example with temperature, just as the speed of the wind varies.

misconceptions.question: A train travels at a constant 45 m/s. How long does it take to cover 9.0 km?
misconceptions.correct: 200 s, from t = s / v with the distance converted to 9000 m.
misconceptions.misconception: The equation s = v t is rearranged the wrong way round, or the kilometres are not converted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students remember the triangle of letters rather than the equation, and the unit conversion is a separate step that is easy to forget once the arithmetic starts.
misconceptions.correction: Rearranging s = v t gives t = s / v. Always convert the distance to metres first when the speed is in m/s.

misconceptions.question: A cyclist rides at 8 m/s for one part of a journey and 12 m/s for another. Is the average speed 10 m/s?
misconceptions.correct: Not necessarily. Average speed is total distance divided by total time.
misconceptions.misconception: The average speed is found by adding the speeds and halving the answer.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word 'average' triggers the arithmetic mean learned in maths, and it happens to give the right answer in the special case where the two stages take equal times.
misconceptions.correction: Average speed for non-uniform motion is total distance travelled divided by total time taken, counting any stops as part of the time.

misconceptions.question: Two cars travel at 20 m/s, one north and one south. Do they have the same velocity?
misconceptions.correct: No. Their speeds are equal but their velocities differ, because velocity includes direction.
misconceptions.misconception: Speed and velocity are interchangeable words, so equal speeds mean equal velocities.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday English the two words are used as synonyms, and in most simple problems only one direction of travel is considered, so nothing forces the distinction.
misconceptions.correction: Velocity is speed in a given direction. Equal speeds in opposite directions are different velocities.

misconceptions.question: A car goes round a roundabout at a steady 8 m/s. Is its velocity constant?
misconceptions.correct: No. The speed is constant but the velocity changes continuously because the direction changes.
misconceptions.misconception: Steady speed round the circle means the velocity is constant too.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Nothing about the motion looks like it is changing - the speedometer reading never moves - and students track the number rather than the direction.
misconceptions.correction: Velocity is a vector, so a change of direction is a change of velocity even when the speed stays the same. Circular motion at constant speed has constantly changing velocity.

misconceptions.question: Part of a distance-time graph is a horizontal straight line. What is the object doing?
misconceptions.correct: It is stationary: the distance is not changing, so the gradient is zero.
misconceptions.misconception: A horizontal line means the object is moving at a constant speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students read 'straight line' as 'steady motion' without looking at the gradient, and a flat line does look like a smooth, unchanging journey.
misconceptions.correction: On a distance-time graph the gradient is the speed. Zero gradient means zero speed; a sloping straight line means constant speed.

misconceptions.question: On a distance-time graph the line passes through the point (40 s, 120 m). What is the speed there?
misconceptions.correct: 3.0 m/s, from the gradient: 120 m divided by 40 s.
misconceptions.misconception: 120 m/s, read straight off the vertical axis.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The vertical axis carries the only number that looks like an answer, and students who have not internalised gradient as rise over run take the coordinate itself.
misconceptions.correction: Speed is the gradient of a distance-time graph - the change in distance divided by the change in time - not the value of the distance at a point.

misconceptions.question: A distance-time graph curves upwards. How is the speed at 6 s found?
misconceptions.correct: By drawing a tangent to the curve at 6 s and measuring the gradient of that tangent.
misconceptions.misconception: By joining the origin to the point on the curve at 6 s and finding that gradient.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The origin-to-point line is what works for a straight graph through the origin, so students carry the method across to a curve without noticing that it now gives an average, not an instantaneous, speed.
misconceptions.correction: For a curved graph the origin-to-point line gives the average speed up to that time. The speed at that instant is the gradient of the tangent drawn at the point.

misconceptions.question: A car speeds up from 5 m/s to 29 m/s in 6.0 s. What is its acceleration?
misconceptions.correct: 4 m/s^2, from the change in velocity, 24 m/s, divided by 6.0 s.
misconceptions.misconception: The final velocity is divided by the time, giving about 4.8 m/s^2.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students recall the equation as 'velocity over time' and the final velocity is the number most visible in the question, so the initial velocity is quietly dropped.
misconceptions.correction: Acceleration = (change in velocity) / (time taken). The change in velocity is final minus initial, here 29 - 5 = 24 m/s.

misconceptions.question: A train slows from 30 m/s to 10 m/s. What does a negative acceleration mean here?
misconceptions.correct: It is decelerating - slowing down while still travelling forwards.
misconceptions.misconception: A negative acceleration means the train is moving backwards.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The minus sign is read as a direction of travel rather than as the direction of the change in velocity, especially when signs are met before vectors are secure.
misconceptions.correction: An object that slows down is decelerating. The acceleration points opposite to the velocity, but the object keeps moving forwards until its velocity reaches zero.

misconceptions.question: Estimate the acceleration of a family car pulling away from traffic lights.
misconceptions.correct: About 2 m/s^2, since it reaches roughly 12 m/s in about 6 s.
misconceptions.misconception: Values such as 100 m/s^2 are quoted, far larger than anything a car can do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students have no reference points for accelerations, and a car pulling away feels dramatic, so any large number seems as good as another.
misconceptions.correction: Check an estimate by multiplying: 2 m/s^2 for 6 s gives 12 m/s, which is a sensible town speed. 100 m/s^2 would reach that speed in about a tenth of a second.

misconceptions.question: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph represent?
misconceptions.correct: The acceleration: the change in velocity divided by the change in time.
misconceptions.misconception: The gradient is read as the distance travelled, or as the speed at that moment.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both graphs have time along the bottom, so students transfer the distance-time rule - gradient is speed - to the velocity-time graph without re-deriving it.
misconceptions.correction: On a velocity-time graph the gradient is the change in velocity divided by the change in time, which is the acceleration.

misconceptions.question: A velocity-time graph rises in a straight line from 0 to 15 m/s over 8.0 s. What distance is travelled?
misconceptions.correct: 60 m, the area of the triangle: half of 8.0 s multiplied by 15 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: 120 m, from base multiplied by height, with the factor of one half left out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Rectangles are the first areas students meet under a velocity-time graph, and the triangle rule is applied without noticing that the shape has changed.
misconceptions.correction: The area of the triangle under the line is half the base times the height. Where the shape is awkward, the area can be measured by counting squares.

misconceptions.question: A car accelerates uniformly at 3.5 m/s^2 from 24 m/s over 7.0 m. What is its final velocity?
misconceptions.correct: 25 m/s, since v^2 = u^2 + 2as = 576 + 49 = 625, and the square root of 625 is 25.
misconceptions.misconception: The square root is never taken, so 625 m/s is quoted, or u^2 is left out so only 2as is used.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is the only one on the sheet with squared terms, and the final step of square rooting is easy to forget once a large number has been produced.
misconceptions.correction: Use v^2 - u^2 = 2as to find v^2, then take the square root. Both velocity terms are squared, so the initial velocity cannot be dropped.

misconceptions.question: Two balls of different mass are dropped together near the Earth's surface. Which accelerates faster?
misconceptions.correct: Neither. Any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2.
misconceptions.misconception: The heavier ball accelerates more because gravity pulls on it harder.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The heavier ball does have a larger weight, and students link larger force to larger acceleration without allowing for its larger mass as well.
misconceptions.correction: Near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2, independent of mass.

misconceptions.question: A skydiver is falling at terminal velocity. What is the resultant force?
misconceptions.correct: Zero: the drag force has grown until it balances the weight.
misconceptions.misconception: Gravity has stopped acting, or the skydiver's weight has become zero.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students associate 'no acceleration' with 'no forces' rather than with balanced forces, so the simplest explanation is that one of the forces has switched off.
misconceptions.correction: At terminal velocity the weight and the drag force are equal and opposite. Both forces are still acting; it is the resultant that is zero.

misconceptions.question: What does a velocity-time graph look like for an object that reaches terminal velocity?
misconceptions.correct: It rises steeply at first, curves as the gradient falls, then levels off as a horizontal line.
misconceptions.misconception: The line rises and then falls back to zero, because the object slows to a stop.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Terminal' sounds like an ending, so students expect the motion to stop rather than to settle at a steady speed.
misconceptions.correction: The graph levels off at the terminal velocity: the object keeps falling at that constant velocity because the resultant force is zero.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of acceleration?
misconceptions.correct: Metres per second squared, m/s^2.
misconceptions.misconception: Acceleration is quoted in metres per second, m/s, the same as velocity.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation contains a velocity in metres per second, and students copy the unit from the numerator rather than working it through the division by time.
misconceptions.correction: Acceleration is a change in velocity divided by a time, so its unit is (m/s) / s, which is m/s^2.

misconceptions.question: A student walks 30 m east then 30 m back to the start. Some say the displacement is 30 m. Why is that wrong?
misconceptions.correct: Displacement is measured from the start point to the finish point, which here are the same point, so it is zero.
misconceptions.misconception: Displacement is the greatest distance the object got from its starting point.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The furthest point reached is a memorable feature of the journey, and it does describe a straight-line distance, so it looks like a displacement.
misconceptions.correction: Displacement depends only on where the object starts and where it ends, not on how far it strayed in between.

misconceptions.question: What does the area under a velocity-time graph represent?
misconceptions.correct: The distance travelled, or the displacement, during that time.
misconceptions.misconception: The enclosed area is taken to be the acceleration.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Acceleration is the quantity students associate with velocity-time graphs, so whichever feature of the graph they are asked about, acceleration is the answer that comes to mind first.
misconceptions.correction: The area under the line is a velocity multiplied by a time, which is a distance. The acceleration is the gradient, not the area.

mcqs.stem: A student walks 30 m due east along a corridor and then walks 30 m back to the point where she started. What are the distance she has travelled and her displacement?

options.text: Distance 60 m; displacement zero, as she ends where she began
options.rationale: Distance is measured along the whole path walked, 30 m + 30 m = 60 m. The straight line from start point to finish point has no length, so the displacement is zero.

options.text: Distance 60 m; displacement 60 m, as both measure her walk
options.rationale: The student treats distance and displacement as the same quantity and quotes the path length twice.

options.text: Distance 60 m; displacement 30 m, the furthest point reached
options.rationale: The student takes the displacement to be how far she got from the start at the furthest point, ignoring the return.

options.text: Distance 30 m; displacement 30 m west, using the return leg
options.rationale: The student uses only the second half of the journey, taking its length as the distance and its direction as the direction of the displacement.

mcqs.stem: A walker sets off from a car park, goes 3.0 km due east and then 4.0 km due north. Which of these correctly expresses her displacement from the car park?

options.text: 7.0 km, on a heading 37 degrees east of north
options.rationale: The magnitudes of the two legs have simply been added instead of being combined as the sides of a right-angled triangle.

options.text: 5.0 km, in a direction 37 degrees east of north
options.rationale: The two legs are at right angles, so the magnitude is the square root of (3.0^2 + 4.0^2) = 5.0 km, and a displacement must also carry the direction of that straight line.

options.text: 5.0 km, and no direction needs to be stated
options.rationale: The magnitude is right, but a displacement is a vector and is not fully expressed until the direction is given.

options.text: 1.0 km, due north of the car park she left
options.rationale: The student subtracts the two legs as though they lay along the same line, as if the walker had doubled back.

mcqs.stem: Which pair contains only scalar quantities?

options.text: Speed and velocity, as both describe how fast it goes
options.rationale: The student treats speed and velocity as the same kind of quantity, missing that velocity carries a direction.

options.text: Distance and displacement, as both are lengths in metres
options.rationale: Both are measured in metres, which the student takes as proof that they are the same kind of quantity.

options.text: Distance and speed, as neither has a direction
options.rationale: Distance is how far an object moves and speed is how fast it moves; neither involves direction, so both are scalars.

options.text: Displacement and velocity, both having a size
options.rationale: The student takes 'has a magnitude' to mean scalar, but these are exactly the two vectors of the group.

mcqs.stem: Which quantity is only fully described when a direction is given as well as a number and a unit?

options.text: Distance, measured along the path
options.rationale: Distance is a scalar; the student assumes that because it is measured in metres it behaves like displacement.

options.text: The time taken, measured in seconds
options.rationale: Time has magnitude only; the student picks a quantity that is simply not a vector.

options.text: Speed, measured in metres per second
options.rationale: The student assumes that because a moving object is going somewhere, its speed must carry a direction.

options.text: Displacement, a vector quantity
options.rationale: Displacement is a vector: it is the straight-line distance from start to finish together with the direction of that line, so both parts must be stated.

mcqs.stem: Two cars travel along the same straight road at 20 m/s, one heading north and the other heading south. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Their speeds are equal but their velocities differ
options.rationale: Speed is a scalar, so both are 20 m/s. Velocity is speed in a given direction, and the directions are opposite, so the velocities differ.

options.text: Their speeds and their velocities are both equal
options.rationale: The student treats speed and velocity as interchangeable words, so equal speeds are taken to mean equal velocities.

options.text: Their speeds differ, but their velocities match
options.rationale: The student attaches the direction to the speed rather than to the velocity, exactly reversing the two.

options.text: Neither their speeds nor velocities are equal
options.rationale: The student assumes that opposite directions must make every quantity different, forgetting that speed ignores direction.

mcqs.stem: Why is the speed of a car driven across a busy town rarely constant?

options.text: Cars are built to hold a single steady speed once moving
options.rationale: The student generalises from textbook problems, which nearly always specify a constant speed.

options.text: The driver keeps changing speed at junctions and bends
options.rationale: The speed of a moving object is rarely constant: when people walk, run or travel in a car their speed is constantly changing.

options.text: Speed can only change when the direction changes too
options.rationale: The student confuses speed with velocity, and so ties any change of speed to a change of direction.

options.text: A speedometer shows the average speed of the trip
options.rationale: A speedometer shows the instantaneous speed; the student mistakes what the instrument reads for a reason the speed is steady.

mcqs.stem: Which list gives factors that affect the speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle?

options.text: Fitness alone, as everybody else walks at 1.5 m/s
options.rationale: The typical value of 1.5 m/s is treated as a fixed figure for everyone rather than as an estimate.

options.text: Terrain and distance only, as age has no effect on it
options.rationale: The student keeps the external factors and drops the ones belonging to the person doing the moving.

options.text: Age, fitness, terrain and the distance travelled
options.rationale: The specification lists age, terrain, fitness and distance travelled among the many factors affecting the speed at which a person can walk, run or cycle.

options.text: Only terrain, since a person's speed is fixed
options.rationale: The student assumes each person has one unchanging speed, so only the ground can alter the journey.

mcqs.stem: Which is the best estimate of the typical speed of a person walking?

options.text: 6.0 m/s, close to 22 km/h
options.rationale: 6 m/s is the typical value for cycling; the student has taken the wrong figure from the list.

options.text: 15 m/s, or roughly 54 km/h
options.rationale: The value is ten times too large; 15 m/s is closer to a car driving through a town.

options.text: 0.15 m/s, or about 0.5 km/h
options.rationale: The value is ten times too small; at 0.15 m/s it would take over an hour to walk 600 m.

options.text: 1.5 m/s, or about 5 km/h
options.rationale: The specification gives walking as about 1.5 m/s, which is roughly 5 km/h - a familiar walking pace.

mcqs.stem: A student is asked to use typical values for the speeds of a runner and a cyclist. Which pair should she use?

options.text: Running about 3 m/s and cycling about 6 m/s
options.rationale: The specification gives running as about 3 m/s and cycling as about 6 m/s, roughly double the running value.

options.text: Running about 6 m/s, cycling about 3 m/s
options.rationale: The two typical values have been swapped over, making the runner faster than the cyclist.

options.text: Running near 3 m/s, cycling near 3 m/s
options.rationale: The student treats the two activities as equally fast, losing the pattern of the typical values.

options.text: Running 1.5 m/s, cycling about 6 m/s
options.rationale: 1.5 m/s is the typical walking speed, not the typical running speed.

mcqs.stem: Which is the most sensible typical speed to quote for a car travelling along a motorway?

options.text: About 300 m/s, which is close to the speed of sound
options.rationale: 330 m/s is the typical speed of sound in air, not of a car; the student has borrowed the wrong typical value.

options.text: About 30 m/s, which is roughly 70 miles per hour
options.rationale: A motorway speed of about 30 m/s is close to 70 mph and is the usual typical value quoted for a car.

options.text: About 10 m/s, a little faster than a cyclist
options.rationale: 10 m/s is only a little above cycling speed and far too slow for a motorway.

options.text: About 3 m/s, about a person's running pace
options.rationale: 3 m/s is the typical running speed; a car on a motorway is about ten times faster.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about the speed of sound in air is correct?

options.text: It is fixed at 300 000 000 m/s in every case
options.rationale: This is the speed of light in a vacuum; the student has confused the two well known speeds.

options.text: It is always exactly 330 m/s, whatever the air
options.rationale: The number is right but the claim is not: the speed of sound in air varies, for example with temperature.

options.text: It varies, but a typical value is 330 m/s
options.rationale: The specification gives a typical value of 330 m/s and notes that the speed of sound, like the speed of the wind, varies.

options.text: It varies, but a typical value is 33 m/s
options.rationale: The typical value is ten times too small; 33 m/s is closer to a car on a motorway.

mcqs.stem: A student sees a flash of lightning and hears the thunder 6.0 s later. Taking the speed of sound in air as 330 m/s, how far away was the lightning?

options.rationale: The student divides the time by the speed instead of multiplying speed by time.
The student uses 33 m/s instead of 330 m/s for the speed of sound in air.
The student divides the speed by the time, giving 330 / 6.0, rather than multiplying.
Using distance travelled = speed × time, s = v t = 330 m/s × 6.0 s = 1980 m.

mcqs.stem: A train travels at a constant speed of 45 m/s. How long does it take to travel 9.0 km?

options.rationale: Rearranging s = v t gives t = s / v. Converting 9.0 km to 9000 m, t = 9000 / 45 = 200 s.
The student multiplies the distance by the speed instead of dividing.
The kilometres are not converted to metres, so 9.0 / 45 is calculated instead of 9000 / 45.
An arithmetic slip of a factor of ten in the division; checking that 20 s at 45 m/s gives only 900 m would catch it.

mcqs.stem: A student wants to measure the average speed of a trolley rolling down a ramp. Which method should she use?

options.text: Measure the distance travelled and the time taken, then multiply these
options.rationale: Multiplying gives a quantity with no useful meaning here; s = v t is being used without rearranging.

options.text: Measure the distance travelled and the time taken, then divide distance by time
options.rationale: Speed is found by making measurements of distance and of time and then dividing the distance by the time taken.

options.text: Measure the distance and the time, then divide the time by the distance
options.rationale: The division is the wrong way round, giving the time taken per metre rather than the speed.

options.text: Measure the time for the trip twice and then find the mean of them
options.rationale: Repeating the timing improves the time measurement but never produces a speed, because no distance is measured.

mcqs.stem: A car's speed changes constantly during a journey through town. How should its average speed for the journey be found?

options.text: Add together the highest and the lowest speeds, then halve that
options.rationale: The student applies the arithmetic mean from maths to the speeds rather than working from totals.

options.text: Divide the total time taken by the total distance moved
options.rationale: The division is inverted, giving seconds per metre instead of metres per second.

options.text: Divide the total distance travelled by the total time taken
options.rationale: Average speed for non-uniform motion is the total distance travelled divided by the total time taken, including any time spent stopped.

options.text: Read the speedometer at the halfway point of the trip
options.rationale: A single instantaneous reading says nothing about the whole journey unless the speed is constant.

mcqs.stem: A cyclist rides 4.0 km in 500 s, rests for 100 s, and then rides 5.0 km in 400 s. What is her average speed for the whole journey?

options.rationale: The student averages the two riding speeds, 8.0 m/s and 12.5 m/s, instead of using the totals.

options.text: 10 m/s
options.rationale: The 100 s rest is left out of the total time, giving 9000 / 900.

options.text: 8 m/s
options.rationale: Only the first stage is used, 4000 m in 500 s, and the rest of the journey is ignored.
Total distance is 9000 m and total time is 1000 s, so the average speed is 9000 / 1000 = 9.0 m/s.

mcqs.stem: Which statement best describes the velocity of a moving object?

options.text: Speed in a given direction
options.rationale: The velocity of an object is its speed in a given direction, which makes velocity a vector quantity.

options.text: Simply another word for speed
options.rationale: The student treats the two words as synonyms, as they often are in everyday English.

options.text: How far it travels each second
options.rationale: This is the definition of speed, offered as though direction were already built into it.

options.text: How quickly its direction changes
options.rationale: The student attaches 'rate of change' to the direction rather than recognising velocity as speed with a direction.

mcqs.stem: Which statement correctly classifies distance, displacement, speed and velocity?

options.text: Distance and displacement are scalars, with the others vectors
options.rationale: The student splits the quantities by their units rather than by whether direction is included.

options.text: Distance and speed are scalars; displacement and velocity are vectors
options.rationale: Distance and speed carry no direction, so they are scalars; displacement and velocity each include a direction, so they are vectors.

options.text: Distance and velocity are scalars, displacement and speed vectors
options.rationale: One member of each pair has been swapped, leaving speed labelled as a vector.

options.text: All four are vectors, since each one has a size and a unit
options.rationale: Having a magnitude is not what makes a quantity a vector; a vector must also have a direction.

mcqs.stem: A car is driven round a roundabout at a steady 8 m/s. Which statement about its motion is correct?

options.text: Both its speed and its velocity stay constant all round
options.rationale: The student watches the unchanging speedometer reading and concludes that nothing about the motion is changing.

options.text: Its velocity is constant but its speed is changing
options.rationale: The two quantities have been swapped, giving the statement exactly the wrong way round.

options.text: Its speed is constant but its velocity keeps changing
options.rationale: Motion in a circle involves constant speed but changing velocity, because the direction of motion changes continuously.

options.text: Neither its speed nor its velocity is constant
options.rationale: The speed is stated as steady in the question, so it cannot be changing.

mcqs.stem: What does the gradient of a distance-time graph tell you about the object?

options.text: The acceleration at that time
options.rationale: Gradient gives acceleration on a velocity-time graph, not on a distance-time graph.

options.text: The distance moved so far
options.rationale: The distance is read from the vertical axis; the gradient is a rate, not a reading.

options.text: The total time of the trip
options.rationale: The time is read from the horizontal axis and has nothing to do with the steepness of the line.

options.text: The speed at that moment
options.rationale: The speed of an object can be calculated from the gradient of its distance-time graph: change in distance divided by change in time.

mcqs.stem: On a distance-time graph a straight line passes through the origin and through the point (8.0 s, 120 m). What is the speed of the object?

options.text: 15 m/s
options.rationale: The gradient is the change in distance divided by the change in time: 120 m / 8.0 s = 15 m/s.
The value on the vertical axis is quoted as the speed instead of the gradient being calculated.
The gradient has been inverted, giving 8.0 / 120 rather than 120 / 8.0.

options.text: 8 m/s
options.rationale: The value on the horizontal axis is quoted instead of the gradient.

mcqs.stem: Part of a distance-time graph for a car is a horizontal straight line. What is the car doing during that part?

options.text: It is moving at a steady speed there
options.rationale: The student reads 'straight line' as 'steady motion' without checking the gradient.

options.text: It is stationary and staying put
options.rationale: A horizontal line has zero gradient, so the distance is not changing and the speed is zero.

options.text: It is going back towards the start
options.rationale: A line returning to the start would slope downwards, not run horizontally.

options.text: It is speeding up all the time
options.rationale: Speeding up would make the line curve upwards and grow steeper.

mcqs.stem: The distance-time graph for an accelerating car is a curve. How should the speed of the car at 6 s be found?

options.text: Join the origin to the point at 6 s and find that gradient
options.rationale: This gives the average speed over the whole six seconds, not the speed at that instant.

options.text: Read the distance at 6 s straight off the vertical axis
options.rationale: This gives a distance in metres, not a speed; no division by time has been done.

options.text: Draw a tangent to the curve at 6 s and measure its gradient
options.rationale: For an accelerating object the speed at a particular time is the gradient of the tangent drawn to the distance-time graph at that time.

options.text: Find the area under the curve up to the 6 s point
options.rationale: Area under a graph is used with velocity-time graphs, and here it would not give a speed.

mcqs.stem: On a distance-time graph the line curves upwards and becomes steeper as time goes on. What does this show?

options.text: The object is slowing down as time goes on
options.rationale: The student reads the rising line as the object tiring, rather than reading the gradient.

options.text: The object moves at a steady high speed
options.rationale: A steady speed gives a straight sloping line, not a curve of increasing steepness.

options.text: The object is moving away from the start
options.rationale: True of any rising line, so it does not explain why the line curves and becomes steeper.

options.text: The object is speeding up as time goes on
options.rationale: An increasing gradient means the distance covered each second is growing, so the object is speeding up.

mcqs.stem: A motorbike speeds up from 5 m/s to 29 m/s in 6.0 s. What is its average acceleration?

options.rationale: Using a = (change in velocity) / t, the change in velocity is 29 - 5 = 24 m/s, so a = 24 / 6.0 = 4 m/s^2.
The time has been divided by the change in velocity, inverting the equation.
The final velocity alone is divided by the time, so the initial velocity is ignored.
The change in velocity is quoted as the answer, with no division by the time, so the unit is wrong as well.

mcqs.stem: A train slows down uniformly from 30 m/s to 10 m/s in 40 s. Which statement is correct?

options.text: It is now travelling backwards along the track at 10 m/s
options.rationale: The minus sign is read as the direction of travel rather than the direction of the change in velocity.

options.text: It is decelerating, and so its acceleration is -0.5 m/s^2
options.rationale: An object that slows down is decelerating. The change in velocity is -20 m/s in 40 s, so the acceleration is -0.5 m/s^2.

options.text: It is decelerating at 0.25 m/s^2, from 10 m/s in 40 s
options.rationale: Only the final velocity has been used instead of the change in velocity.

options.text: It is accelerating at 0.5 m/s^2 along the track
options.rationale: The magnitude is right but the sign is not: the velocity is falling, so the acceleration opposes the motion.

mcqs.stem: Which is the best estimate of the acceleration of a family car pulling away from traffic lights?

options.text: About 100 m/s^2, so reaching 12 m/s in around 0.1 s
options.rationale: This would take the car to town speed in about a tenth of a second, which no car can do.

options.text: About 9.8 m/s^2, the same as an object falling
options.rationale: 9.8 m/s^2 is the acceleration of free fall, far greater than a family car can manage.

options.text: About 2 m/s^2, reaching some 12 m/s in about 6 s
options.rationale: A sensible everyday estimate: 2 m/s^2 sustained for 6 s gives 12 m/s, a reasonable town speed.

options.text: About 0.02 m/s^2, reaching 12 m/s in 10 min
options.rationale: The estimate is a hundred times too small; the car would barely creep forward.

mcqs.stem: What does the gradient of a velocity-time graph give?

options.text: The distance it has travelled
options.rationale: The gradient is a rate of change, not a reading of how far the object has gone.

options.text: The speed it has at that moment
options.rationale: The speed is read from the vertical axis; the student carries across the distance-time graph rule.

options.text: The average velocity so far
options.rationale: Average velocity comes from the values on the vertical axis, not from the steepness of the line.

options.text: The object's acceleration
options.rationale: The acceleration of an object can be calculated from the gradient of a velocity-time graph.

mcqs.stem: A velocity-time graph for a cyclist is a straight line rising from 0 m/s to 15 m/s over 8.0 s. What distance does the cyclist travel in that time?

options.rationale: The distance is the area under the line, a triangle: 0.5 × 8.0 s × 15 m/s = 60 m.
The gradient has been calculated, which gives the acceleration rather than the distance.
The average velocity has been found but never multiplied by the time, so the answer is not a distance.
Base multiplied by height has been used, leaving out the factor of one half for a triangle.

mcqs.stem: A car accelerates uniformly at 3.5 m/s^2 from an initial velocity of 24 m/s over a distance of 7.0 m. What is its final velocity?

options.rationale: The factor of 2 has been left out, giving v^2 = 576 + 24.5 and a final velocity of about 24.5 m/s.

options.text: 25 m/s

options.rationale: The value of v^2 has been quoted as the answer without taking the square root.

options.text: 7 m/s
options.rationale: Only 2 a s has been used and then square rooted, so the initial velocity has been dropped.

mcqs.stem: A ball is dropped near the Earth's surface. Ignoring air resistance, what is its acceleration as it falls?

options.text: About 9.8 m/s^2 if the ball is heavy
options.rationale: The student links the greater weight of a heavy object to a greater acceleration, forgetting its greater mass.

options.text: About 9.8 m/s, growing as the ball falls
options.rationale: The unit given is that of velocity, and free fall has a constant acceleration, not a growing one.

options.text: About 9.8 m/s^2, directed downwards
options.rationale: Near the Earth's surface any object falling freely under gravity has an acceleration of about 9.8 m/s^2.

options.text: Zero, as it falls at steady speed
options.rationale: The student assumes balanced forces from the start, but a freely falling ball speeds up throughout.

mcqs.stem: A skydiver falling through the air reaches terminal velocity. Which statement describes what is happening?

options.text: Gravity has stopped acting, so no force acts at all now
options.rationale: The student links zero acceleration to zero force rather than to balanced forces.

options.text: The skydiver slows down and stops falling in the air
options.rationale: 'Terminal' is read as 'coming to an end', but the skydiver keeps falling at a steady velocity.

options.text: The air resistance is now larger than the skydiver's weight
options.rationale: If drag exceeded the weight the skydiver would slow down, so the velocity would not be constant.

options.text: The resultant force is zero, so velocity is steady
options.rationale: The drag force grows as the skydiver speeds up until it balances the weight; with zero resultant force the velocity stays constant.
